newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Q1 growth bodes well for 1997 target.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Q1 growth bodes well for 1997 target.

text.p: With Argentina's economy expanding by a stronger-than-expected 8.1 percent in the first quarter, the government seems more likely to achieve its goal of six percent growth for the year, analysts said Wednesday.
"I am not surprised by the figure," said Sergio Galvan, head of research at Bansud. "We expect growth of more than seven percent."

Earlier, the Economy Ministry said first-quarter gross domestic product grew 8.1 percent compared with growth of 8.8 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 and a 3.2 percent contraction in the first quarter of last year.
Analysts on average forecast first-quarter growth at 7.4 percent, according to a Reuters poll.
The Economy Ministry also revised its estimate of 1996 growth to 4.3 percent from 4.4 percent.

Raul Buonuome, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said he may slightly increase his 1997 growth estimate of 5.7 percent in view of revised 1996 growth figure and the economy's stronger-than-expected first-quarter performance.
ING Barings on Tuesday said it revised its 1997 Argentine growth forecast to 6.6 percent from 5.2 percent.
The GDP data rounded off a series of figures released this week showing an increasingly healthy economy, with rising exports and investment fueling non-inflationary expansion.
Figures released late Tuesday showed consumer prices fell 0.3 percent in April, the third consecutive month of deflation. Wholesale prices fell 0.4 percent in the month.

Also on Tuesday, the Economy Ministry reported tax collections in May reached $4.6 billion, a record high since the 1991 introduction of the so-called Convertibility Plan, which fixes the Argentine peso at par with the dollar.
Another analyst who asked not to be named said the strong tax revenues bode well for Argentina's chances of meeting second-quarter deficit targets agreed with the International Monetary Fund.

Argentina's stand-by accord with the IMF sets a 1997 deficit target of $3 billion. The country met the first-quarter target with a deficit of $1.04 billion. The second-quarter deficit target is $360 million.

While many analysts now believe 1997 growth could meet the government's six percent target, they said growth in the remaining quarters would probably fall short of the first quarter's 8.1 percent pace.
